title: WHAT IF YOU ACCEPTED JESUS… BUT THE SIN HE CAME TO SAVE YOU FROM IS STILL THE ONE YOU REFUSE TO SURRENDER?
paragraphs: WHAT IF YOU ACCEPTED JESUS… BUT THE SIN HE CAME TO SAVE YOU FROM IS STILL THE ONE YOU REFUSE TO SURRENDER?

You prayed the prayer. You called Him Lord. You believe He died for your sins. But what happens when you want His forgiveness without His authority, His promises without repentance, and His heaven without allowing Him to change your heart? The answer may disturb you—but it could also be the very truth that saves you from a lifetime of spiritual deception.
There is a terrifying possibility that many people sitting in churches have never seriously considered.
You can know the songs.
You can memorize the verses.
You can raise your hands during worship, cry during an altar call, post Scripture on Facebook, and tell everyone that Jesus Christ is your Lord and Savior.
And still be resisting the very Lord you claim to follow.
Not because you struggle.
Not because you sometimes fall.
Not because your transformation is taking longer than you hoped.
But because somewhere deep inside, you have made a decision that you rarely say out loud.
“Jesus, You can save me. But You cannot touch this part of my life.”
And perhaps the most frightening thing about that sentence is how easily it can hide behind religious language.
You say, “God knows my heart.”
And He does.
You say, “Nobody is perfect.”
And nobody is.
You say, “We are saved by grace, not by works.”
And that is gloriously true.
But what happens when you begin using those beautiful truths to protect the very sins Jesus died to deliver you from?
What happens when grace becomes your explanation for refusing repentance?
What happens when the Savior is welcome, but the King is not?
Before you answer, there is something you need to understand.
This is not a story about someone who has fallen and desperately wants to get back up.
It is about someone who has become comfortable staying down.
And the difference between those two hearts may be greater than you realize.
Imagine a man sitting alone in his car outside a church.
The worship service has just ended.
His Bible is on the passenger seat. His eyes are wet. During the sermon, he felt something he had not felt in months—a piercing awareness that God was confronting something in his life.
He knows exactly what it is.
The dishonesty nobody knows about.
The relationship he refuses to leave.
The bitterness he keeps feeding.
The pornography he has stopped fighting.
The pride that makes every correction feel like an attack.
The secret habit he has learned to defend instead of confess.
For one brief moment, he considers surrendering it.
Then his phone lights up.
A familiar notification.
An invitation back into the very thing he knows is destroying him.
He looks at his Bible.
Then at his phone.
And quietly whispers, “Lord, You understand.”
He drives away.
Nothing changes.
The next Sunday, he returns to church.
He sings the same songs.
He hears the same truth.
He feels the same conviction.
And makes the same decision.
Again.
And again.
Until one day, the thing that once made him tremble barely troubles him anymore.
That is where this conversation becomes painfully serious.
Because the greatest danger is not always that sin suddenly destroys your life.
Sometimes it is that repeated resistance slowly teaches your heart to stop listening.
Hebrews 3:13 warns believers about being hardened through the deceitfulness of sin.
Notice that expression.
The deceitfulness of sin.
Sin does not always arrive announcing, “I am here to ruin your relationship with God.”
Sometimes it whispers, “Just this once.”
Then, “You deserve this.”
Then, “Everyone does it.”
Then, “God will forgive you anyway.”
Eventually, it no longer needs to whisper.
You have learned to argue on its behalf.
And that is when a person can begin mistaking spiritual numbness for spiritual peace.
Jesus spoke directly to this danger.
In Luke 6:46, He asked:
“And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?” — Luke 6:46, KJV
In the Greek text, the question begins:
Τί δέ με καλεῖτε· Κύριε κύριε, καὶ οὐ ποιεῖτε ἃ λέγω;
Ti de me kaleite, Kyrie kyrie, kai ou poieite ha legō?
The word Κύριε (Kyrie) means “Lord,” a form of address recognizing someone as master or one possessing authority.
Jesus repeats the address as His hearers do: “Lord, Lord.”
And then He exposes the contradiction.
Why do you call Me your Lord while refusing to do what I say?
He is not suggesting that imperfect obedience automatically cancels salvation.
He is confronting the emptiness of a profession that refuses to acknowledge His authority.
You cannot reduce Jesus to someone who pays the penalty for your rebellion while you permanently reserve the right to remain rebellious.
The Gospel offers something infinitely greater than that.
It offers reconciliation with God.
Forgiveness.
A new heart.
A new life.
And a new relationship with the One you once resisted.
But here is where many sincere Christians become afraid.
They hear a message about obedience and immediately wonder:
“Does this mean I am not saved because I still struggle?”
“Does this mean Jesus has rejected me because I keep falling?”
“Does this mean I have to become perfect before God will accept me?”
No.
Please hear that clearly.
You are not saved because you successfully changed yourself. You are saved by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — KJV
The Greek word translated “grace” is χάρις (charis).
It speaks of favor and gift, and in this passage emphasizes that salvation originates in God's generosity, not in human achievement.
You cannot earn the cross.
You cannot purchase forgiveness with moral improvement.
You cannot make yourself worthy of Christ's blood.
If salvation depended upon your flawless performance, nobody would have hope.
But Paul does not end his explanation at verse nine.
The very next verse says:
“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.” — Ephesians 2:10, KJV
Do you see the beauty of that?
Good works are not the price of salvation.
They are part of the new life for which God creates us in Christ.
We are not saved by good works.
We are saved for a life in which good works have their rightful place.
And that changes the entire conversation.
Because the question is no longer, “Have I become perfect enough for Jesus to love me?”
The question becomes, “If I truly trust Jesus as Savior and Lord, why am I determined to keep Him away from the very place where I need His transforming grace?”
There is a difference between a Christian who hates the sin they keep falling into and a person who loves the sin they have decided to keep.
Both may outwardly look similar for a season.
Both may confess the same failure.
Both may experience repeated temptation.
But one is crying, “Lord, deliver me.”
While the other is saying, “Lord, leave this alone.”
God alone knows the heart perfectly, and no observer can infallibly determine someone's salvation from a single struggle.
Still, Scripture repeatedly warns that settled, unrepentant rebellion must never be treated as spiritually harmless.
Consider what the apostle Paul wrote in Romans 6:1–2:
“What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid. How shall we, that are dead to sin, live any longer therein?” — KJV
The Greek response is unforgettable:
μὴ γένοιτο (mē genoito).
Often rendered “God forbid” in the King James Version, this expression communicates Paul's emphatic rejection: “Absolutely not!” or “May it never be!”
Paul anticipates the argument people still make today.
If God's grace is greater than sin, why not keep sinning?
If Jesus forgives, why change?
If salvation is a gift, why surrender anything?
Paul's answer is not that grace is insufficient.
His answer is that such reasoning fundamentally misunderstands what union with Christ means.
Christ did not die merely to make rebellion consequence-free.
He died and rose again so that those who belong to Him might share in newness of life.
Grace is not God's permission to remain enslaved.
Grace is His undeserved favor that brings forgiveness and begins transforming those who receive it.
And sometimes that transformation begins with the most painful sentence a person can speak:
“Lord, I have been calling this weakness when I know I have been defending it.”
Maybe that sentence is difficult for you.
Maybe you have been living with a secret contradiction for years.
You love Jesus—or at least you believe you do.
You believe the Bible.
You know the Gospel.
But there is one part of your life you keep negotiating with God about.
You want Him to bless your relationship without confronting its dishonesty.
You want Him to restore your family without asking you to abandon your pride.
You want Him to heal your heart without surrendering your bitterness.
You want peace without confession.
Freedom without accountability.
Forgiveness without repentance.
And perhaps you have become so skilled at explaining your behavior that you no longer recognize how deeply it is wounding you and the people around you.
But listen.
God's confrontation is not necessarily evidence that He has abandoned you.
It may be the very mercy that is calling you home.
The conviction that exposes your sin can also become the doorway through which you return to the Savior.
Remember Peter.
He promised loyalty to Jesus.
He spoke with confidence.
He believed he was ready to suffer for his Lord.
Then, when the pressure came, he denied knowing Him.
Not once.
Three times.
And when the rooster crowed, Peter remembered Jesus' words.
Luke 22:62 records something devastating:
“And Peter went out, and wept bitterly.”
Imagine that moment.
The man who had confidently declared his devotion was now confronted by his own cowardice.
His words had collapsed.
His courage had failed.
His love had been exposed as weaker than he imagined.
Yet Peter's failure was not the final chapter of his story.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored Peter in a deeply personal encounter recorded in John 21.
Jesus did not pretend the denial had never happened.
He addressed Peter's love and recommissioned him to care for His sheep.
That is grace.
Not grace that calls denial good.
Not grace that teaches Peter to remain comfortable with cowardice.
Grace that meets a fallen disciple, restores him, and calls him forward.
Now consider Judas.
He too walked with Jesus.
He heard the teachings.
He witnessed extraordinary things.
He lived near the truth.
Yet proximity to Jesus did not automatically mean surrender to Jesus.
Judas betrayed Him.
And although Matthew 27 describes Judas experiencing remorse, the Gospel does not portray his story as the same restoration we see in Peter.
We should not reduce these two men to a simplistic formula about tears or emotions. Their stories are more profound than that.
But together they confront us with a sobering reality.
Religious association is not the same thing as living faith.
Feeling terrible about what happened is not necessarily the same as turning to Christ.
And failure does not have to be the end when a sinner returns to the mercy of Jesus.
That brings us to a word that many modern believers misunderstand.
Repentance.
In Mark 1:15, Jesus proclaimed:
“The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel.” — KJV
The Greek verb translated “repent” is μετανοεῖτε (metanoeite), from metanoeō.
It means to repent, involving a change of mind or understanding that, in biblical context, entails a genuine turning toward God.
It is not merely feeling embarrassed after being caught.
It is not simply crying because consequences have arrived.
It is not promising to change so that God will temporarily stop confronting your conscience.
Repentance is a real reorientation of the heart toward God.
And genuine repentance bears fruit in life, even though growth may be uneven and the battle against sin may be long.
Repentance does not mean you will never be tempted again.
It does not mean every addiction disappears overnight.
It does not mean trauma, entrenched habits, or destructive patterns are resolved through one emotional prayer.
Some battles require sustained discipleship, trusted accountability, pastoral care, and appropriate professional support.
But repentance does mean you stop treating sin as something you are entitled to protect.
You bring it into the light.
You confess it.
You seek help.
You begin taking concrete steps of obedience.
When you fall, you return to Christ instead of declaring the battle unnecessary.
And when change feels impossible, you do not pretend that God's commands have become irrelevant.
You ask Him for the grace to continue.
This is why 1 John 1:9 is such a lifeline:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — KJV
The Greek verb ὁμολογῶμεν (homologōmen) means “we confess” or “we acknowledge.”
Confession is not a performance designed to impress God.
It is truthful acknowledgment before the One who already knows us completely.
You do not have to manufacture a spotless spiritual record before approaching Him.
You come honestly.
Without excuses.
Without pretending.
Without calling darkness light.
And you come trusting the cleansing that God promises through Christ.
But there is another passage we cannot ignore simply because it makes people uncomfortable.
Matthew 7:21–23.
Jesus warns that not everyone who says to Him, “Lord, Lord,” will enter the kingdom of heaven.
Some will point to remarkable religious works done in His name.
Yet Jesus describes a devastating separation between outward profession and truly belonging to Him.
Think about how sobering that is.
These are not people who never heard His name.
They speak His name.
They appeal to spiritual activity.
They appear confident in their religious credentials.
But the passage confronts the terrible possibility of mistaking visible ministry or religious performance for a genuine relationship with Christ.
The warning is not that true believers must earn God's acceptance through sinless perfection.
Nor does it give us permission to announce who is eternally lost based on our suspicions.
It tells us something we desperately need to hear.
A confident claim to know Jesus is not, by itself, proof that we belong to Him.
That is why the apostle Paul calls believers to examine themselves in 2 Corinthians 13:5.
Not to become trapped in endless, hopeless introspection.
Not to measure salvation by emotional intensity.
But to take seriously the reality of faith in Christ.
And this examination must always lead us back to Jesus Himself.
Not to the strength of our willpower.
Not to the number of religious activities we perform.
Not to our ability to appear righteous.
To Christ.
Because salvation is found in Him.
And here is something else we must confront.
Some people say they refuse to change because they are afraid of becoming hypocrites.
They tell themselves, “I would rather be honest about my sin than pretend to be holy.”
There is something important in that concern.
God does not ask us to manufacture religious appearances.
But honesty about sin is not the same as repentance from sin.
Admitting that you are holding a poisonous cup does not make continuing to drink from it wise.
And refusing to pretend is not a reason to refuse healing.
The answer to hypocrisy is not to abandon holiness.
The answer is to come into the light with humility.
Jesus' grace does not require you to hide your wounds.
It invites you to bring them to the One who can heal.
Perhaps the most revealing question is not whether you have changed enough.
Perhaps it is this:
When Jesus confronts something in your life, do you ultimately want to obey Him—or do you want Him to stop confronting you?
Read that again.
Slowly.
Because there are people who have spent years asking God to remove the consequences of choices they have no intention of changing.
They ask Him to save their marriage while continuing the betrayal.
They ask Him to restore trust while continuing the lies.
They ask Him to bless their finances while continuing deliberate dishonesty.
They ask Him to give them peace while nurturing resentment.
They ask Him to make them spiritually strong while refusing the ordinary means of growth He has provided.
And when the consequences arrive, they wonder why life feels so painful.
Not every hardship is punishment for personal sin. Jesus Himself rejects simplistic assumptions about suffering in John 9:1–3.
But our choices do matter.
Sin can wound relationships, destroy trust, harden our consciences, and bring consequences that do not disappear simply because we use religious language.
God's forgiveness is real.
So is the damage sin can cause.

And sometimes repentance means accepting responsibility for harm we have done, making appropriate restitution where possible, and allowing trust to be rebuilt through consistent truthfulness over time.
That is not earning forgiveness.
That is refusing to use forgiveness as an excuse to keep hurting people.
Now we need to speak about one of the most beautiful promises in all of Scripture.
Ezekiel 36:26.
God declares:
“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.” — KJV
In the Hebrew text, the expression for “a new heart” is:
לֵב חָדָשׁ (lev chadash).
Lev means “heart,” and chadash means “new.”
In biblical Hebrew, the heart is not merely the center of emotion. It is deeply associated with a person's inner life, thinking, desires, and will.
God's promise, originally spoken in the context of Israel's restoration, reveals His intention to renew His people inwardly rather than merely demand outward conformity.
And Christians recognize its profound relationship to the new-covenant transformation made possible through Christ and the Spirit.
Think about what that means.
God does not merely stand at a distance shouting, “Change yourself!”
He promises a work of inward renewal.
He gives His Spirit.
He changes what we love.
He teaches us to hate what once enslaved us.
He creates desires that did not previously govern our lives.
And that process of sanctification continues as believers learn to walk in obedience.
But we must not confuse God's transforming power with a promise of instant perfection.
Even mature Christians still need repentance.
Even devoted disciples can fail.
Even those who genuinely love Christ may experience seasons of weakness, grief, confusion, or spiritual exhaustion.
The difference is not that authentic Christians never fall.
The difference is that the Gospel does not teach them to make peace with remaining in rebellion.
First John 2:1 beautifully holds both truths together.
John writes so that believers will not sin.
Then he immediately reminds them that if anyone does sin, Jesus Christ the righteous is our advocate with the Father.
Do you hear the balance?
Do not embrace sin.
And when you sin, do not abandon hope.
Run to your Advocate.
Jesus is not standing before the Father hoping your good behavior will finally outweigh your failures.
His saving work is sufficient.
His righteousness is not defective.
His mercy is not fragile.
And because His grace is real, you no longer need to defend what is destroying you.
You can confess it.
You can turn from it.
You can begin again.
Not because sin is small.
But because Christ is mighty to save.
There is a scene in John 8 that captures something precious about the heart of Jesus.
A woman accused of adultery is brought before Him.
Her accusers are ready to use her shame as a weapon.
Jesus confronts their hypocrisy, and one by one they depart.
Then He speaks to the woman.
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11, KJV

The account of the woman caught in adultery, John 7:53–8:11, has a well-known textual history: the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John do not contain it, and many modern Bibles identify this passage accordingly. We should be transparent about that rather than build an entire doctrine upon a disputed passage.
Nevertheless, its picture of mercy joined with a call to holiness is consistent with the wider, securely attested teaching of Jesus and the apostles.
Mercy is not permission to continue destroying yourself.
And the call to leave sin is not a denial of mercy.
Both belong together.
Jesus does not invite sinners to despair.
He invites them to follow Him.
That invitation may cost you something.
It may cost a relationship that continually pulls you away from obedience.
It may cost the approval of people who preferred the old version of you.
It may cost habits that have become emotional hiding places.
It may cost pride.
It may cost comfort.
It may require an apology you have avoided for years.
It may require telling the truth when a lie would be easier.
It may require seeking help for something you have been ashamed to admit.
And yes, following Jesus may require you to surrender things that once seemed inseparable from your identity.
But what are you truly losing when Christ frees you from what is killing your soul?
Jesus asks in Mark 8:36:
“For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?” — KJV
There is a kind of success that hides spiritual ruin.
A kind of comfort that conceals bondage.
A kind of religion that allows a person to remain unchanged while feeling safely surrounded by Christian language.
And there is a kind of surrender that feels like losing everything until you discover that Christ Himself is your greatest treasure.
Perhaps you are reading this and something inside you has become unsettled.
Not because you hate Jesus.
But because you recognize yourself.
You remember when sin troubled you more deeply.
When prayer was honest.
When you wanted God's will even when it hurt.
When you could not easily excuse what you now tolerate.
And somewhere along the way, you became tired.
Tired of resisting temptation.
Tired of failing.
Tired of confessing the same thing.
Tired of feeling disappointed in yourself.
So instead of returning to Jesus with your exhaustion, you slowly lowered your expectations of obedience.
You told yourself that this was simply who you were.
You stopped believing real change was possible.
And eventually you began calling surrender unrealistic.
If that is you, please hear this.
You do not have to choose between pretending you are holy and surrendering to hopelessness.
There is another way.
Come to Jesus as you are.
But do not insist that He leave you as you are.
Bring Him the exhausted heart.
The recurring failure.
The secret shame.
The hardened attitude.
The habit you have been too embarrassed to name.
The resentment that has become part of your personality.
Bring Him even your unwillingness to change.
And pray honestly:

“Lord, I know Your Word is right, but my heart is resisting You. I cannot pretend otherwise. Give me a willing heart. Teach me to hate what is evil and love what is good. Help me take the next faithful step.”
That is not a polished prayer.
It is an honest one.
And honesty before God is a far better beginning than a thousand impressive religious words spoken to conceal the truth.
Philippians 2:12–13 reminds believers to work out their salvation with fear and trembling because God is at work in them, both to will and to work for His good pleasure.
Notice the extraordinary relationship.
God works within His people.
And His people are called to respond actively.
His grace does not make obedience unnecessary.
His grace makes a new life possible.
You are not being invited to rescue yourself.
You are being called to trust the Savior who rescues sinners and transforms His people.
And transformation does not always look dramatic.
Sometimes it looks like deleting a number you know you should never call again.
Sometimes it looks like admitting the truth to your spouse.
Sometimes it looks like choosing not to retaliate.
Sometimes it looks like walking away from a conversation designed to feed your pride.
Sometimes it looks like opening your Bible when you feel spiritually empty.
Sometimes it looks like calling a mature believer and finally saying, “I need help.”
Sometimes it looks like getting up after another failure and refusing to let shame convince you that Jesus has no mercy left.
These steps do not purchase salvation.
They are ways of responding to the Lord who calls us to follow Him.
And if you are truly following Him, the direction of your life matters even when your progress feels painfully slow.
Now imagine that man in the car again.
The one outside the church.
The one staring at his phone.
The one who keeps saying, “Lord, You understand.”
Imagine that this time, something changes.
The notification appears.
The temptation is familiar.
His heart begins producing the same excuses.
But instead of driving away, he places the phone down.
He bows his head.
And for the first time in a long time, he stops negotiating.

“Jesus,” he whispers, “I don't want to give this up. That's the truth. Part of me still loves it. But I know it is wrong. I know it is pulling me away from You. And I am tired of pretending that I can keep both my rebellion and my peace.”
He begins to cry.
Not because he has suddenly become strong.
But because he has finally stopped pretending he is.
“Please change my heart.”
Nothing spectacular happens.
No thunder.
No visible miracle.
No instant guarantee that temptation will never return.
But he makes a call to someone he trusts.
He confesses what he has been hiding.
He asks for accountability.
He takes the first costly step away from the pattern he has been defending.
And tomorrow, he will need grace again.
And the next day.
And the next.
But something essential has changed.
He is no longer asking Jesus to bless his refusal to surrender.
He is asking Jesus to teach him how to obey.
That is not the completion of sanctification.
It is a picture of repentance beginning to bear fruit.
And perhaps that is the very step God is calling you to take today.
Not a dramatic promise that you will never struggle again.
Not a public performance of spirituality.
Not a desperate attempt to earn what Christ has already accomplished.
Just honest surrender.
A genuine turning.
A willingness to stop protecting the thing that is harming your relationship with God and others.
Because here is the answer to the question we began with.
What happens when someone accepts Jesus but refuses to change?

We must first distinguish between someone who professes faith but deliberately rejects repentance and someone who genuinely belongs to Christ yet struggles through a long and difficult process of growth.
Scripture does not teach that every struggling believer is unsaved.
Nor does it teach that saying a prayer or making a religious profession guarantees salvation regardless of a person's settled rejection of Christ's lordship.
Persistent, defended rebellion is spiritually dangerous.
It can harden the heart.
It can reveal that a profession of faith is empty.
It calls for serious self-examination and repentance.
Yet we must not claim to know every person's eternal condition. Final judgment belongs to God, who knows the heart.
And for anyone who hears His call today, the invitation of the Gospel remains glorious.
Repent.
Believe in Jesus Christ.
Receive His mercy.
Follow Him.
Do not attempt to turn your obedience into the price of His love.
But do not turn His love into permission to reject His authority.
The same Savior who forgives sinners also calls them into new life.
And the power to live that new life comes from Him.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — KJV
The Greek phrase καινὴ κτίσις (kainē ktisis) means “new creation.”
It speaks of the profound new reality of belonging to Christ.
Not merely a better public image.
Not merely a religious label.
Not merely a cleaned-up version of the same self-directed life.
New creation.
And that newness is rooted in Jesus—His death, His resurrection, and the saving work of God.
The person who once found refuge in hiding can learn to walk in truth.
The person enslaved by bitterness can learn forgiveness.
The person consumed by pride can learn humility.
The person who once defended sin can learn to confess it.
Not all at once.
Not without struggle.
Not without tears.
But through the transforming grace of God.
This is why the Gospel is not simply the story of bad people becoming respectable.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again, as Paul declares in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
It is the good news that sinners can be reconciled to God through Him.
It is the promise that condemnation does not have the final word over those who are in Christ Jesus.
It is the invitation to leave behind the old life and walk in the new.
And this is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior.
Not because scandal was harmless.
Not because our sins were imaginary.
Not because God lowered His holiness to accommodate our rebellion.
But because Jesus entered our broken world, bore our sins, conquered death, and opened the way for guilty people to receive forgiveness and become new.
The scandal of our sin is real.
The grace of our Savior is greater.
And the life He calls us into is worth surrendering everything to follow.
If this article has exposed something you have been hiding, I want to invite you to respond—not for appearances, not to prove your salvation to strangers, but as a simple expression of honesty.

And if God has already brought you through a season of repentance and restoration, consider sharing a little of your testimony. Someone reading the comments may be convinced that their failures have placed them beyond the reach of mercy.
Your testimony could remind them that Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
We want this community to be a place where Scripture is taken seriously, repentance is preached with compassion, grace is never cheapened, and Jesus Christ remains the center of everything.
There is a great deal of Christian content available online.
But what people need is more than another inspirational quote that disappears from memory after a few seconds.
They need the Word of God.
They need sound teaching.
They need encouragement grounded in truth.
They need to be reminded that Christ calls sinners to repentance and gives grace to those who come to Him.
They need resources that help them keep growing after the emotional moment has passed.
Our desire is to keep making biblical nourishment available, especially to those who are hungry for God's Word but may not have the means to purchase Christian resources.
If you have been blessed by this ministry and have the financial ability to support it, we would be grateful to have you walk alongside us.
Not because giving money makes you more spiritual.
Jesus Christ has already accomplished what no financial gift could ever accomplish.
It is a voluntary expression of generosity toward a ministry you believe is serving others.
Scripture teaches believers to give willingly, not under pressure. Second Corinthians 9:7 says that giving should not be done grudgingly or out of necessity, for God loves a cheerful giver.
These items are not the reason to give.
They are simply one way we can say thank you for helping this ministry continue.
You can help this message reach someone without spending anything.
One private message can begin a conversation about repentance.
One testimony can encourage someone who thought they were alone.
We cannot know what every act of kindness will accomplish.
But we can faithfully offer what we have and entrust the results to God.
Before you leave, however, I want to return to the question that started everything.
What happens when someone accepts Jesus but refuses to change?
The most urgent issue is not whether you can convince others that you are a Christian.
It is whether you are genuinely trusting the Jesus revealed in Scripture, rather than a version of Him who never challenges your rebellion.
He is not merely a comforting addition to your existing life.
He is the crucified and risen Lord.
The One who forgives.
The One who commands.
The One who restores.
The One who transforms.
And the One who is worthy of your trust.
Maybe tonight you need to stop defending something.
Maybe you need to confess a lie.
Maybe you need to make a phone call.
Maybe you need to ask forgiveness.
Maybe you need to return to prayer after months of silence.
Maybe you need to seek help because the battle has become too heavy to fight in isolation.
Or maybe you need to stop measuring God's willingness to receive you by the number of times you have failed.
Remember the promise of John 6:37:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — KJV
Those are the words of Jesus.
Come to Him.
Not with the illusion that you have no sin.
Not with the demand that He must approve everything you do.
Come trusting His mercy and yielding to His truth.
If you have never truly placed your faith in Him, hear the Gospel today.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, died for sinners and rose again.
Forgiveness and eternal life are found in Him.
Turn to Him in repentance and faith.
And if you already belong to Him but have wandered, do not make your failure your permanent home.
Return to the Shepherd.
He is worthy of your surrender.
He is worthy of your obedience.
And His grace is sufficient for the journey ahead.
Let this be your prayer:

“Lord Jesus, I have called You Savior, but there are places in my life where I have resisted Your authority. Forgive me for the sins I have defended and the excuses I have made. I cannot save myself, and I cannot transform my heart by my own strength. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Teach me to trust You, to repent sincerely, and to follow You faithfully. Give me courage to confess what I have hidden, wisdom to seek help where I need it, and humility to take the next step of obedience. Thank You that Your grace is greater than my failures and that Your truth is better than my excuses. Let my life increasingly reflect the mercy and holiness of the One who saved me. In Your name, Jesus. Amen.”
And if you are still reading, perhaps there is one final question you need to answer—not to me, not to the comments, not to anyone watching your life.
To God.
What have you been asking Jesus to forgive while refusing to let Him confront it?
You do not have to announce the answer publicly.
But do not keep hiding it from yourself.
Bring it before Him.
Because the deepest tragedy would not be discovering that you still have much growing to do.
It would be spending your life defending the chains from which Jesus came to set you free.
The Savior who welcomes you in your brokenness loves you too much to call your chains your freedom.
